{{short description|Native American politician (1939–2014)}}
{{Use American English|date=July 2026}}
'''Bender "Ben" Johnson Jr.''' (May 22, 1939 – March 31, 2014) was an American [[Makah]] politician and [[fisheries]] expert. He served as the chairman and member of the [[Makah Reservation|Makah Tribal Council]] from 1998 until 2000 and from 2001 until 2007.<ref name=pdn>{{cite news|first=Rob|last=Ollikainen |title=Former Makah tribal chairman dead at 74 |url=http://www.peninsuladailynews.com/article/20140404/NEWS/304049978/former-makah-tribal-chairman-dead-at-74 |work=[[Peninsula Daily News]] |date=2014-04-03 |access-date=2014-05-17}}</ref> He was chairman of the Makah during the first successful [[whaling|hunt]] of a [[Gray whale|Pacific gray whale]] in 1999.<ref name=pdn/>  The 1999 hunt, which took a 30-ton  30 1/2-foot female gray whale, was the first harvest of a whale by the Makah since the 1920s.<ref name=pdn/><ref name=nytimes/> Johnson supported the hunt, which drew worldwide attention and controversy.<ref name=pdn/><ref name=nytimes>{{cite news|first=Sam |last=Howe Verhovek |title=After the Hunt, Bitter Protest and Salty Blubber |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1999/05/19/us/after-the-hunt-bitter-protest-and-salty-blubber.html |work=[[The New York Times]] |date=1999-05-19 |access-date=2014-05-17}}</ref>

==Early life and education==
Ben Johnson was born on May 22, 1939, in [[Neah Bay, Washington]], to parents Bender Johnson Sr. and Harriet Eliot Stewart.  At the age of five, he began fishing with his father and grandfather, which sparked his lifelong career in the fishing industry; his devotion to fishing was often described as "his life" <ref name=pdn/> Johnson spent most of his life in Neah Bay, with the exception of a two-year period when he left to study at [[Peninsula College]] in nearby [[Port Angeles, Washington]].<ref name=pdn/>At Peninsula College, he obtained an [[associate degree]], a [[fisheries]] [[technician]] degree and several professional certifications. <ref name=pdn/><ref name=legacy>{{cite news|title=Obituary: Ben Johnson (May 22, 1939 - March 31, 2014) |url=http://www.legacy.com/obituaries/peninsuladailynews/obituary.aspx?n=ben-johnson&pid=170479976 |work=[[Legacy.com]] |publisher=[[Peninsula Daily News]] |date=2014-04-04 |access-date=2014-05-17}}</ref>

==Career==
After leaving Peninsula College, Johnson worked as a [[biologist]] for the now defunct U.S. Bureau of Commercial Fisheries (which has since merged into the present-day [[National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration]]). He worked on board a Bureau [[research vessel]], the George B. Kelez, in the [[Bering Sea]].<ref name=pdn/>

Johnson soon returned to Neah Bay, where he lived for the rest of his life.<ref name=pdn/> He devoted much of his professional life to serving the Makah and the [[Makah Reservation]], specifically in tribal government and the fishing industry. He worked as the personnel officer, [[general manager]], fisheries [[assistant director]] and fisheries director.<ref name=pdn/> He also served as the Makah director of fisheries, member of the Makah Housing Authority, and the executive director of the Makah Tribe Youth Program.<ref name=pdn/><ref name=legacy/>

Johnson first served on the Makah Tribal Council from 1998 and 2000.<ref name=pdn/> He declined to seek re-election, citing the controversy surrounding the 1999 whale hunt while he was chairman.<ref name=pdn/> Johnson won re-election in 2001, serving as a council member and chairman until 2007.<ref name=pdn/>

The Makah had retained the right to practice [[whaling]] under the [[Treaty of Neah Bay]] in 1855, the only tribe in the [[continental United States]] to do so.<ref name=pdn/> The Makah stopped whaling in the 1920s due to the decline of the gray whale population, but decided to resume the harvest in the 1990s after the Pacific gray whale was removed from the [[Endangered Species Act|list]] of [[endangered species]] in 1994.<ref name=pdn/> Whale meat had been a vital component of the diet of the Makah people for hundreds of years.<ref name=pdn/> Johnson, a proponent of the 1999 hunt, worried that the cultural significance of whaling would be lost on younger Makah members if the harvest did not resume.<ref name=pdn/> In a 2009 [[interview]] with the ''[[Peninsula Daily News]]'', Johnson reflected on the long-term significance of the 1999 hunt on the Makah, "I should feel happy about that day, but I'm not because we have people that are still against us...It gets old. We don't want to stir the pot again. People don't like to hear the truth. We have to think about things like that. We [the Makah] are [[whaler]]s."<ref name=pdn/>

==Death==
Johnson died at the age of 74 on March 31, 2014, at [[Olympic Medical Center]] following a heart attack.<ref name=pdn/> He was survived by his wife, Jeanne Johnson, five children, thirty grandchildren, and fifty-one great-grandchildren.<ref name=pdn/>
